overview.explanation: Dashed arrows show compile-time dependencies on a type or function. There is no inheritance and no heap ownership in this example.

focus.title: State what equality means
focus.code:
struct UserId{ int value; };
bool operator==(UserId a, UserId b){ return a.value==b.value; }
explain: struct creates the UserId type. Its value member is public by default. The semicolon ends the type declaration.
operator== defines equality for two UserId values. The parameters are copies; comparing their integer fields produces a bool result.
focus.what: The wrapper gives a name and type to the meaning “user identifier.”
focus.where: The declarations appear before the call in main, so the compiler can resolve a==b.
focus.why: The type makes intent visible. For a small identifier, copying is simpler than managing pointers.
focus.invariant: Two identifiers with the same value compare equal. Equality must be consistent wherever the type is used.
focus.risk: Comparing addresses would compare objects’ locations rather than identifier values. A public field allows arbitrary integers, so this type alone does not enforce valid user ranges.

focus.title: Call the type’s equality operation
focus.code: int main(){ UserId a{7}, b{7}; std::cout << std::boolalpha << (a==b) << '\n'; }
explain: Braces initialize two separate UserId objects with the value 7. a==b calls the overload. std::boolalpha makes the stream print true instead of 1, followed by a newline.
focus.what: The caller observes equality without depending on the comparison’s spelling.
focus.where: This is the entry point and the complete output-producing call.
focus.why: A named type helps separate user identifiers from unrelated integers in larger interfaces.
focus.invariant: Both objects live until main returns; no reference escapes. The expected output is true.
focus.risk: Changing operator== to compare another property changes every caller’s meaning of equality.
